evidence.claim: US 20 runs through Wind River Canyon between walls that rise as much as 2,500 feet, with three road tunnels cut through Precambrian rock.

evidence.claim: Designated a Wyoming Scenic Byway in 2005, the corridor crosses the Wind River Indian Reservation.
evidence.quote: It was designated as a Wyoming Scenic Byway in 2005.

evidence.claim: Travel Wyoming highlights the rock layers identified by roadside signs and gives a nonstop drive time of about 40 minutes.
evidence.quote: The geology of every layer is marked by interpretive signage, making the drive a geology lesson and a trip through time.

evidence.claim: The river’s course predates the uplift of the Owl Creek Mountains, cutting through them as the land rose.
evidence.quote: The canyon was cut in the established course of the Wind River, which predates the uplift of the Owl Creek Mountains. The water gap was created as the topography of the mountains was raised

evidence.claim: Work on the canyon road began in 1922 and finished in 1924, replacing the route over Bird’s Eye Pass.
evidence.quote: Work on U.S. 20/Wyo 789 through Wind River canyon began in 1922 and was finished in 1924, replacing the Bird's Eye Pass Route over the Owl Creek Mountains.

evidence.claim: Construction preparations for Boysen Dam later required relocation of both US 20 and the Chicago, Burlington and Quincy Railway.
evidence.quote: the relocation of U.S. Highway 20 and the Chicago, Burlington and Quincy Railway to bypass the construction site.

evidence.claim: Traveling south, begin at the Thermopolis end and pass the Wedding of the Waters, where the river’s name changes between Bighorn and Wind.
evidence.quote: The north end of the canyon is at the Wedding of the Waters, where the Wind becomes the Bighorn River. The Scenic Byway continues for several miles through Thermopolis

evidence.claim: Continue through the canyon toward Boysen Dam at its southern mouth.
evidence.quote: The southern mouth of the canyon is near the Boysen Dam

evidence.claim: Beyond Boysen Reservoir, the route reaches Shoshoni, with the yellow and red rocks of the Owl Creek Mountains beside this part of the drive.
evidence.quote: As you travel north from Shoshoni into BoysenState Park

evidence.claim: Beyond Boysen Reservoir, the route reaches Shoshoni, with the yellow and red rocks of the Owl Creek Mountains beside this part of the drive.
evidence.quote: You can see the bare yellow and red rock of the Owl Creek Mountains stretching off to forever, and the deep blue of Boysen Reservoir

evidence.claim: At the north end of the canyon, the Wind River becomes the Bighorn without meeting another stream.
evidence.quote: where the north-flowing Wind River becomes the Bighorn River, an instance of a river changing names at a point other than a confluence of two streams.

evidence.claim: The name Wedding of the Waters dates to at least 1934, when a marker was placed here.
evidence.quote: The term "Wedding of the Waters" dates to at least 1934, when a marker was placed at the location.

evidence.claim: The water flows north from Boysen Reservoir through the canyon, then through Thermopolis.
evidence.quote: The Wind and Big Horn flow north out of Boysen Reservoir, through the canyon, into Thermopolis

evidence.claim: Wind River is the name applied to the Bighorn’s upper reaches.
evidence.quote: The Wind River is the name applied to the upper reaches of the Bighorn River in Wyoming

evidence.claim: Forty-three bighorn sheep reached the canyon in 1995 by an unusual combination of road and rail.
evidence.quote: 1995 saw 43 bighorns &ldquo;transplanted&rdquo; along the canyon rim.

evidence.claim: They traveled from Dubois in horse trailers, then rode the final seven miles on railroad flatcars before release in the canyon.
evidence.quote: After making the trip from Dubois, WY in horse trailers, the sheep were then loaded onto flatcars by Burlington-Northern Railroad before traveling the final 7 miles by railroad. They were released in the canyon

evidence.claim: The highway itself runs at canyon-floor level in places, with views of Chimney Rock.
evidence.quote: U.S. 20/Wyo 789 travels through the canyon, at times level with the canyon floor. The scenic route offers views of the canyon and landmark natural structures like the Chimney Rock.

evidence.claim: Roadside signs identify exposed strata, including a sequence of rock layers cut by a river older than the uplift of the Owl Creek Mountains.
evidence.quote: The canyon cuts through a comprehensive set of Wyoming rock strata exposures. Many of these are noted on roadside signs. The canyon was cut in the established course of the Wind River, which predates the uplift of the Owl Creek Mountains.

evidence.claim: Boysen Dam holds back the reservoir at the head of Wind River Canyon, supplying irrigation water, flood control and hydroelectric power.
evidence.quote: The dam lies at the head of Wind River Canyon through the Owl Creek Mountains in western Wyoming and creates Boysen Reservoir. It is owned by the U.S. Bureau of Reclamation and furnishes irrigation water supply to the Bighorn Basin as well as providing flood control and hydroelectric power.

evidence.claim: An earlier concrete dam, built under Asmus Boysen’s supervision in 1908, silted up and was removed in 1948.
evidence.quote: The first dam to be built at the Wind River Canyon site was actually in 1908, when Asmus Boysen supervised the construction of a small concrete run-of-the-river structure

evidence.claim: The replacement required a railway tunnel beneath the dam and part of the future reservoir, 7,131 feet long.
evidence.quote: the railway, which would run under the dam and portions of the future reservoir through a tunnel 7,131 feet (2,174 m) long.

evidence.claim: That tunnel opened in September 1950; the new dam was completed in February 1952.
evidence.quote: the train tunnel was completed and opened on September 5, 1950

evidence.claim: An earlier concrete dam, built under Asmus Boysen’s supervision in 1908, silted up and was removed in 1948.
evidence.quote: This early dam, located just downriver of the present Boysen Dam, silted up by 1925 and was removed in 1948.

evidence.claim: That tunnel opened in September 1950; the new dam was completed in February 1952.
evidence.quote: the entire dam was completed on February 16, 1952

evidence.claim: Roadside signs identify the canyon’s exposed rock layers.
evidence.quote: The canyon cuts through a comprehensive set of Wyoming rock strata exposures. Many of these are noted on roadside signs.

evidence.claim: The reservation is shared by the Eastern Shoshone and Northern Arapaho.
evidence.quote: is shared by two Native American tribes, the Eastern Shoshone (Shoshoni: Gweechoon Deka, lit. 'Buffalo Eaters') and the Northern Arapaho

evidence.claim: On this southbound journey, red sandstone at the canyon’s northern end gives way to cliffs of limestone, dolomite and sandstone before the tunnels in Precambrian rock.
evidence.quote: Beyond the tunnels, the strata dip, with high cliffs of sedimentary Madison Limestone, Bighorn Dolomite and sandstone. The northern end of the canyon cuts through red sandstone of the Chugwater Formation.

evidence.claim: At the southern tunnels the canyon narrows into Precambrian rock; farther north, high cliffs expose Madison Limestone, Bighorn Dolomite and sandstone.
evidence.quote: then narrows as it descends into Precambrian rocks at three road tunnels. Beyond the tunnels, the strata dip, with high cliffs of sedimentary Madison Limestone, Bighorn Dolomite and sandstone.

evidence.claim: When the river’s diversion tunnel was sealed in October 1951, the new reservoir began to rise behind the embankment.
evidence.quote: on October 11, 1951, the diversion tunnel was sealed and Boysen Reservoir began to rise.

flags: Road dates and geology have only secondary-source support in the cache. Construction dates refer to the canyon road, not proof that the numbered US route existed under that name in 1922.
Wedding of the Waters is short because the supported naming story is simple; no claim that its 1934 marker survives.
Tribal names match the reservation cache. No tribal-community source is cached, so the story does not add cultural interpretation or promise off-highway access.
